1.4 SELECTION SORT: The "Pick the Best" Algorithm

Selection sort works differently from bubble sort. Instead of comparing neighbors and swapping, selection sort actively searches for the smallest (or largest) element and moves it to its correct position. Imagine picking team members by always choosing the shortest person first, then the next shortest from those remaining.

THE SELECTION SORT CONCEPT:

Selection sort divides the list into two parts: sorted and unsorted. It repeatedly finds the smallest element from the unsorted part and moves it to the end of the sorted part.

HOW SELECTION SORT WORKS:

1. Look at the entire unsorted list and find the smallest element

2. Remove it from the unsorted list

3. Add it to the end of the sorted list

4. Look at the remaining unsorted elements and find the next smallest

5. Move it to the sorted list

6. Repeat until all elements are sorted

DETAILED SELECTION SORT EXAMPLE:

Sorting: [5, 2, 8, 1]

STEP 1: Find smallest in [5, 2, 8, 1]

Smallest is 1

→ [1 | 5, 2, 8]

STEP 2: Find smallest in remaining [5, 2, 8]

Smallest is 2

→ [1, 2 | 5, 8]

STEP 3: Find smallest in remaining [5, 8]

Smallest is 5

→ [1, 2, 5 | 8]

STEP 4: Only 8 remains

Add to sorted

→ [1, 2, 5, 8] ✓ DONE!

1.5 INSERTION SORT: The "Card Game" Algorithm

Insertion sort is the algorithm you naturally use when sorting playing cards. As you pick up each new card, you insert it into the correct position among the cards you're already holding. This algorithm is especially efficient for small lists or data that's already partially sorted.

THE INSERTION SORT CONCEPT:

Insertion sort maintains a sorted section and an unsorted section. For each element in the unsorted section, it finds the correct position in the sorted section and inserts it there.

HOW INSERTION SORT WORKS:

1. Start with the first element (it's trivially sorted)

2. Take the next element from the unsorted section

3. Compare it with elements in the sorted section from right to left

4. Shift larger elements one position to the right

5. Insert the element in its correct position

6. Move to the next unsorted element

7. Repeat until all elements are sorted

DETAILED INSERTION SORT EXAMPLE:

Sorting: [5, 2, 8, 1] (Sorted | Unsorted parts marked with |)

INITIAL: [5 | 2, 8, 1]

(5 is already sorted)

INSERT 2: Where does 2 go in [5]?

2 < 5? YES → 2 goes before 5

Result: [2, 5 | 8, 1]

INSERT 8: Where does 8 go in [2, 5]?

8 < 5? NO → 8 goes after 5

Result: [2, 5, 8 | 1]

INSERT 1: Where does 1 go in [2, 5, 8]?

1 < 8? YES → shift 8 right

1 < 5? YES → shift 5 right

1 < 2? YES → shift 2 right

Result: [1, 2, 5, 8] ✓ SORTED!

1.6 MERGE SORT: The "Divide & Conquer" Champion

Merge sort is fundamentally different from the first three algorithms. Instead of directly sorting by comparing and moving elements, merge sort uses a divide-and-conquer strategy: split the data into smaller pieces, sort each piece, then merge them back together. This approach is much faster for large datasets.

THE DIVIDE & CONQUER STRATEGY:

The "divide and conquer" approach breaks a large problem into smaller subproblems, solves each subproblem independently, then combines the solutions. For sorting, this means: split the data in half repeatedly until each piece has just one element (trivially sorted), then merge pieces back together in sorted order.

WHY DIVIDE & CONQUER WORKS FOR SORTING:

1. A single element is already sorted (trivial case)

2. Merging two sorted lists is easy—just compare elements from each list

3. By repeatedly dividing and merging, we efficiently sort the entire list

4. The number of merge operations is logarithmic, making it fast

HOW MERGE SORT WORKS:

1. DIVIDE PHASE: Keep dividing the list in half until each piece has one element

2. This creates a tree structure of divisions

3. MERGE PHASE: Start merging pieces back together

4. When merging two sorted lists, compare the first element of each

5. Take the smaller element and add it to the result

6. Move forward in whichever list you took from

7. Continue until both lists are empty

8. The result is a sorted merged list

DETAILED MERGE SORT EXAMPLE:

Sorting: [5, 2, 8, 1]

PHASE 1: DIVIDE (Split into individual elements)

[5, 2, 8, 1]

↓ Split in half

[5, 2] and [8, 1]

↓ Split again

[5] [2] [8] [1] ← Each element alone!

PHASE 2: MERGE (Combine back in sorted order)

Merge [5] and [2]: Compare 5 vs 2 → 2 < 5 → [2, 5]

Merge [8] and [1]: Compare 8 vs 1 → 1 < 8 → [1, 8]

Merge [2, 5] and [1, 8]: → [1, 2, 5, 8] ✓ FULLY SORTED!

1.7 COMPLETE ALGORITHM COMPARISON

Now that we've studied all four algorithms, let's compare them across important dimensions:

Aspect Bubble Selection Insertion Merge Winner
Speed (1000 items) SLOW SLOW Medium FAST! MERGE
Memory Used Low Low Low Higher Top 3
Stable? Yes ✓ No ✗ Yes ✓ Yes ✓ MERGE
Best For Learning Teaching Nearly sorted Production MERGE

KEY INSIGHTS FROM THE COMPARISON:

✓ Bubble and Selection Sort are similar in speed—both O(n²)—but Selection needs fewer swaps

✓ Insertion Sort excels when data is nearly sorted (common in real applications!)

✓ Merge Sort trades memory for speed—uses extra memory but is significantly faster

✓ For real-world applications, Merge Sort (or similar fast algorithms) is essential

STUDY QUESTIONS - Test Your Understanding:

1. Explain why Merge Sort is faster than Bubble Sort for large datasets.

2. When would you use Insertion Sort instead of Merge Sort?

3. What does 'stable sort' mean and why might it matter?

4. Trace through Merge Sort on the list [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]

DATA & ANALYSIS

Master Study Guide

Grade 7-8 Computer Science

What is Data?

Data is INFORMATION. Numbers, text, measurements—anything that describes something.

Examples: "Sarah is 5'4", "It's 75°F today", "I watched 3 TikTok videos". All data!

Why Does Data Matter?

  • Netflix uses data to recommend shows you'll like

  • Banks analyze data to detect fraud

  • Doctors use patient data to make diagnoses

  • Meteorologists analyze weather data for forecasts

The Big Four: MEAN, MEDIAN, MODE, RANGE

MEAN (Average)

  • Add all numbers, divide by how many numbers

  • Example: [10, 20, 30] → (10+20+30)÷3 = 20

MEDIAN (Middle)

  • Sort data, find the middle value

  • Example: [3, 5, 8] → median is 5 (middle)

MODE (Most Common)

  • The value that appears most often

  • Example: [1, 2, 2, 3] → mode is 2

RANGE (Spread)

  • Largest value - Smallest value

  • Example: [5, 15] → range is 10 (15-5)

Data Cleaning: Making Messy Data Perfect

Real data is MESSY. Before analyzing, we need to clean it!

What We Fix:

  • Typos and misspellings

  • Duplicates (two identical entries)

  • Missing values

  • Outliers (extreme values that don't belong)

After Cleaning?

  • Data is consistent and ready for analysis!

Key Terms

DATASET

  • A collection of related information or measurements

OUTLIER

  • An unusual value that doesn't fit the pattern

FILTER

  • Show only data that meets certain conditions

SORT vs FILTER

  • SORT = Arrange in order | FILTER = Show only matching data

COMPUTING SYSTEMS

Master Study Guide

Grade 7-8 Computer Science

Hardware vs Software

HARDWARE (You can touch)

  • CPU (processor) - the brain

  • RAM (memory) - temporary storage

  • Hard drive - permanent storage

  • Monitor, keyboard, mouse, printer

SOFTWARE (You cannot touch)

  • Windows, macOS, Linux

  • Chrome, Firefox, Safari

  • Games, apps, programs

  • Your photos, documents, videos

The Computer's Brain & Memory

CPU (Central Processing Unit)

  • Executes instructions and does calculations

  • Speed measured in GHz (Gigahertz)

RAM (Random Access Memory)

  • FAST temporary memory (clears when powered off)

  • Holds programs you're currently running

  • More RAM = smoother multitasking

STORAGE (Hard Drive/SSD)

  • PERMANENT - keeps data even when off

  • Slower than RAM but holds much more

Input & Output Devices

INPUT (From You → Computer)

  • Keyboard, mouse, touchscreen, microphone

OUTPUT (From Computer → You)

  • Monitor, printer, speakers, headphones

Remember

  • INPUT = You give information TO the computer

  • OUTPUT = Computer sends information TO you

Binary: Computer's Secret Code

Computers only speak in 0s and 1s. Everything is stored as binary!

  • 0 = OFF (no electrical signal)

  • 1 = ON (electrical signal)

Examples:

  • 5 decimal = 101 binary

  • 8 decimal = 1000 binary

  • Letter A = 01000001 binary

Troubleshooting Steps

Computer being slow? Try these in order:

  • 1 RESTART - Turn it off and on again

  • 2 CHECK - Plugged in? WiFi connected?

  • 3 CLOSE - Too many programs open? Close some

  • 4 UPDATE - Install latest software

  • 5 ASK FOR HELP - Call tech support

Binary Operations

Ready to check yourself?Take the individual test

Place values in binary

Binary uses only two digits, 0 and 1. Each place is worth double the place to its right. For an 8-bit number the places are:

1286432168421
10110000

The example above is 128 + 32 + 16 = 176. To convert a number, add up the place values that have a 1 under them.

Adding binary

Add column by column, from right to left, just like decimal. Remember two rules:

  • 1 + 1 = 10 (write 0, carry 1)
  • 1 + 1 + 1 = 11 (write 1, carry 1)

Example: 1111 + 0001. The right column gives 1 + 1 = 10, so write 0 and carry 1. Each column after that carries, and the result is 10000, which is 15 + 1 = 16.

Shifting bits

A right shift moves every bit one place to the right. Each shift divides the value by 2. A left shift moves bits left and multiplies by 2. Shifting 0110 (6) right gives 0011 (3).

AND and OR

These compare two numbers bit by bit:

  • AND gives 1 only when both bits are 1.
  • OR gives 1 when either bit is 1.

Example: 1100 AND 1010 = 1000. Example: 1100 OR 1010 = 1110.

How many values fit?

With n bits you can make 2n different patterns. Six bits make 26 = 64 patterns. In 8-bit two's complement, the largest positive value is 127 (01111111), because the leftmost bit is reserved for the sign.

Letters are numbers too

Computers store letters as numbers using a code called ASCII. Uppercase A is 65, which is 01000001 in binary. Lowercase a is 97.

Home/New guides

Hexadecimal Numbers

Ready to check yourself?Take the individual test

What is hexadecimal?

Hexadecimal, or hex, is a base-16 number system. It uses the digits 0 to 9 and then the letters A to F:

Hex0-9ABCDEF
Decimal0-9101112131415

Place values

Each place is worth 16 times the place to its right. Hex 2A means 2 × 16 + 10 = 42. Hex 7C means 7 × 16 + 12 = 124.

Hex and binary

One hex digit stands for exactly four binary bits. This makes hex a short way to write binary:

Hex01234567
Binary00000001001000110100010101100111
Hex89ABCDEF
Binary10001001101010111100110111101111

Example: 11010110 splits into 1101 and 0110, which are D and 6. So 11010110 = D6.

Where you will see hex

  • Colors: #RRGGBB. In #00FF00 the green part is at maximum (FF) and the others are zero, so it is pure green. #000000 is black.
  • Memory addresses: long binary addresses are shorter and easier to read in hex.
  • Character codes: lowercase a is 97 in decimal, which is 61 in hex.

Online Safety and Security

Ready to check yourself?Take the individual test

Strong passwords and password managers

Use a long password that you do not reuse anywhere else. A password manager creates unique passwords for every account and stores them securely, so you only need to remember one master password.

Two-factor authentication

Two-factor authentication (2FA) asks for a second proof of identity, such as a code sent to your phone or made by an app. Even if someone steals your password, they still need the second factor.

Phishing

Phishing is a trick to get you to share information, usually by pretending to be someone you trust. Common types include:

  • Phishing by email
  • Smishing: phishing by text message (SMS)
  • Vishing: voice phishing by phone call
  • Spear phishing: a targeted attack that uses personal details to seem believable

Malware and keyloggers

A keylogger secretly records what you type, which can expose passwords and messages. Install software only from trusted sources, and be careful with browser extensions, since they can often read the pages you visit.

After a data breach

Change the passwords for affected accounts, turn on two-factor authentication, and watch for suspicious activity.

VPNs and public Wi-Fi

A VPN encrypts the traffic between your device and the VPN server. It helps protect you on public networks, though it does not stop phishing or stop you from sharing a password.

Cyberbullying

If you see cyberbullying, report it through the platform and support the person being targeted. Do not share the harmful content.

Software Uses

Ready to check yourself?Take the individual test

Match the job to the tool

Every program is designed for certain jobs. Knowing the main use of each one helps you pick the right tool quickly.

JobCommon tools
Formatted writing (essays, reports)Microsoft Word, Google Docs
Plain text with no formattingNotepad
Calculations and tables with formulasMicrosoft Excel
Slide presentationsMicrosoft PowerPoint, Microsoft Sway (web-based stories)
Surveys and quizzesGoogle Forms
Posters and graphics from templatesCanva
Photo editingAdobe Photoshop
Video editing (timelines)Adobe Premiere Pro
3D models and animationBlender
Playing audio and videoVLC Media Player
Learning to code with blocksScratch
Tracking tasks on a boardTrello
Video calls and team chatMicrosoft Teams
Tracking changes to codeGit (version control)

Collaboration

Tools like Google Docs let several people edit one document at the same time, with comments and version history. Teams combines video calls, chat, and file sharing in one app.

Think about the purpose

Notepad is best when you do not want any formatting. Word and PowerPoint add formatting that may not be wanted in a plain note. Excel is built for math across large tables, not for layout.

Home/New guides

Multimedia Basics

Ready to check yourself?Take the individual test

Raster or vector?

A raster image is a grid of pixels. PNG and JPEG are raster formats. It can look blurry when enlarged.

A vector image is made of mathematical paths and shapes. SVG is a vector format. It scales to any size without losing sharpness.

Choosing a file format

  • JPEG (.jpg): good for photographs with many colors. It discards some detail to save space.
  • PNG (.png): good for screenshots, logos, and images with text or sharp edges.
  • SVG (.svg): good for icons and logos that must scale.

Bitrate

Bitrate is the number of bits used each second to store audio or video. A higher bitrate usually means better quality and a bigger file.

Codecs

A codec is software or hardware that encodes (compresses) media for storage and decodes it for playback. H.264 is a common video codec. Heavy compression can cause compression artifacts, which are blocky or blurry areas.

Video basics

  • A video is a rapid sequence of frames, each one a still image.
  • The aspect ratio describes the shape of the picture. 16:9 is standard widescreen.
  • Stereo audio uses two channels: left and right.
  • Video editors such as Adobe Premiere Pro arrange clips, audio, and effects on a timeline.
Home/New guides

Sorting Algorithms

Ready to check yourself?Take the individual test

Why sorting matters

Sorting puts items in order so they are easier to search and use. Computer scientists compare sorting methods by how many steps they take as the list grows. We use n for the number of items.

Simple sorts

  • Bubble sort swaps neighbors that are out of order. Its worst case is about n² steps. If a full pass makes no swaps, the list is sorted and it can stop early, which gives O(n) on a sorted list.
  • Selection sort finds the smallest item and moves it to the front, then repeats. It always makes about n²/2 comparisons, no matter the input order.
  • Insertion sort builds a sorted section one item at a time. It is very fast on lists that are already nearly sorted.

Faster sorts

  • Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half, and merges them. It always takes about n log n steps, but it needs extra memory for merging.
  • Quick sort picks a pivot and splits the list around it. On average it is n log n, but a bad pivot can make it n².
  • Heap sort uses a binary heap to remove the largest or smallest item again and again.
  • Radix sort sorts numbers one digit place at a time, without comparing whole numbers.

Stable sorts and searching

A stable sort keeps equal items in their original order. A binary search on a sorted list of 1,024 items needs at most 10 comparisons, because log₂ 1024 = 10. Linear search on an unsorted list may check all n items.

Home/New guides

Data and Analysis

Ready to check yourself?Take the individual test

Three measures of center

  • Mean: add all values and divide by how many there are. The mean of 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 is 30 ÷ 5 = 6.
  • Median: the middle value after sorting. For 3, 4, 7, 9, 12 the median is 7. For an even count, average the two middle values.
  • Mode: the value that appears most often.

The median is less affected by an extreme outlier, because it depends only on position.

Spread

Range is the maximum minus the minimum. Standard deviation measures how far values usually sit from the mean.

Types of data

Categorical data describes a category, like favorite color. Numerical data is measured, like height. A sample is a smaller group studied to learn about a larger population.

Charts

  • Use a line graph to show change over time.
  • Use a pie chart to show parts of a whole.

Correlation is not causation

Two variables can move together without one causing the other. A correlation of 0 means there is no straight-line relationship between them.

In a spreadsheet

=SUM(A1:A3) adds the cells. =AVERAGE(A1:A5) returns their mean.

Home/New guides

Computing Systems

Ready to check yourself?Take the individual test

Inside the CPU

The CPU is the processor that runs instructions. Its main parts are the control unit, which directs the work; the arithmetic logic unit, which does math and logic; and registers, the fastest storage in the computer.

The instruction cycle

The CPU repeats three steps: fetch an instruction, decode it, then execute it.

Speed and cores

  • Clock speed is measured in hertz. A 3 GHz CPU completes about 3 billion cycles per second.
  • A quad-core CPU has four processing cores, so it can work on four tasks at once.
  • Pipelining overlaps the steps of several instructions to finish more work per cycle.

Memory from fastest to slowest

Registers are fastest, then cache, then RAM, then storage such as an SSD or hard drive. Cache sits closer to the CPU, so it is faster than RAM. An SSD has no spinning parts, so it is faster than a hard disk drive.

Other parts

  • A GPU runs many calculations in parallel, mainly for graphics.
  • A bus is a set of wires that carries data between parts.
  • The power supply converts household AC power into the DC power components use.
  • Firmware, such as BIOS, is software stored on a chip that starts and controls the hardware.
  • The operating system manages hardware and software resources, including memory and devices.
Home/New guides

Networking and the Internet

Ready to check yourself?Take the individual test

Addresses

  • An IP address identifies a device on a network, so data can be sent to it.
  • A MAC address is built into a network card and identifies that interface on a local network.
  • A subnet mask shows which part of an IP address is the network and which is the device.
  • DHCP assigns IP addresses automatically. ARP finds the MAC address for a known IP address.

Moving data

Data is split into small packets that can take different routes and be reassembled at the destination. This is called packet switching.

  • TCP checks delivery and order, and resends lost data.
  • UDP skips those checks to stay fast.
  • A switch sends frames only to the device they are addressed to. A hub repeats traffic to every port.
  • Traffic for other networks goes to the default gateway, usually the router.

Ports

Ports help a computer sort incoming traffic. HTTPS uses port 443, email sending uses 25, FTP uses 21, and DNS uses 53.

Speed words

Bandwidth is how much data can move per second. Latency is how long a packet takes to arrive.

Cloud computing

Cloud computing means using servers you reach over the internet to store files and run software.

Home/New guides

Internet Usage

Ready to check yourself?Take the individual test

Domains and HTTPS

In https://www.example.com/page, the domain is example.com. The https:// part means the connection is encrypted. A padlock and a valid certificate confirm that the site is secure. DNS turns the domain name into an IP address.

Search engines

Search engines use crawlers to visit pages and store them in an index. Results come from that index.

  • Quotation marks find an exact phrase.
  • A minus sign before a word leaves out pages with that word.

Browser basics

  • A cookie is a small text file a site saves to remember things such as your login.
  • The cache stores copies of web files. Clearing it can fix loading problems.
  • Private browsing stops your browser from saving history and cookies on that device. It does not hide you from websites or your internet provider.
  • Browser extensions can often read the pages you visit, so install only trusted ones.

Status codes

CodeMeaning
200OK: the page was found and sent
301The page has moved permanently
404The page could not be found
500The server hit an internal error
Home/New guides

Communications

Ready to check yourself?Take the individual test

Email

  • To holds the main recipients. CC sends a copy. BCC hides recipients from one another.
  • The subject line tells readers what the message is about.
  • Reply All sends to everyone on the original message, so use it only when everyone needs the reply.
  • SMTP sends email. IMAP and POP3 let your email app retrieve it. IMAP keeps mail synced on the server across devices.

Synchronous and asynchronous

Synchronous communication happens in real time, like a live video call. Asynchronous communication does not need both people at once, like email or a voicemail.

Calls and chat

  • VoIP carries voice calls as data over the internet.
  • High latency or low bandwidth causes lag and dropped audio on video calls.
  • Written chat leaves a record you can review later. A thread groups related messages together.

Good netiquette

Use a clear subject, a respectful tone, and avoid ALL CAPS. Before you send a large file to a group, ask whether everyone needs it, or share a link instead. If you get a message meant for someone else, tell the sender and delete it.

Home/New guides

Digital Citizenship

Ready to check yourself?Take the individual test

What it means

Digital citizenship is using technology in a responsible, ethical, and safe way. It also means being able to find, judge, and use information well, which is called digital literacy.

Copyright and licenses

  • Copyright protects original creative works, not ideas or facts.
  • Fair use allows limited quoting for purposes such as review or commentary, with credit.
  • CC BY lets others share and adapt a work if they credit the creator.
  • CC0 means no rights are reserved. Anyone can use the work for any purpose.

Plagiarism

Copying words is plagiarism, and so is paraphrasing an idea without a citation. Always cite the sources of ideas and quotations.

Judging sources

Be careful with content that has no author, no date, and no sources. Checking your own name online shows your digital footprint.

Access and accessibility

  • The digital divide is the gap in access to devices, internet, and skills.
  • Alt text describes an image so screen readers can speak it aloud to people who cannot see it.

Responsibility

Deepfakes can make realistic fake media of real people, which can spread false information. Old electronics contain hazardous materials, so recycle them responsibly.

Home/New guides

Impacts of Computing

Ready to check yourself?Take the individual test

Jobs and automation

Automation can raise productivity, but it changes which jobs are available. Repetitive, rule-based tasks are the easiest to automate.

Privacy

  • Combining data sets, called data aggregation, can reveal sensitive details about a person.
  • Facial recognition can identify people without their knowledge or consent.

Bias and fairness

Algorithmic bias happens when biased data or design choices produce unfair results for some groups. Algorithms learn patterns from data, so they can repeat unfair patterns.

Environment

Data centers use large amounts of electricity and often water for cooling. Training large AI models also uses a lot of energy. Planned obsolescence designs products to wear out or become outdated sooner, which adds electronic waste.

Society

  • Remote work can reduce commuting for some workers.
  • Online shopping has shifted spending away from some traditional stores.
  • Smart cities use sensors and data to improve traffic, utilities, and services.
  • Open-source software lets anyone inspect, change, and share the code.
  • Misinformation spreads fast when engagement-driven recommendations promote it.
  • Students without home internet can fall behind on online work. Captions help many viewers, not only people who are deaf.
Home/New guides

History of Computing

Ready to check yourself?Take the individual test

Early ideas

Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine in the 1830s, a general-purpose mechanical computer that was never completed. Konrad Zuse built the Z3 in 1941, one of the first working programmable computers.

Electronic computers

  • First-generation computers such as ENIAC (completed in 1945) used vacuum tubes, which were large, hot, and failure-prone.
  • Transistors, invented at Bell Labs in 1947, were smaller, more reliable, and used less energy.
  • The Intel 4004 (1971) was the first commercial microprocessor, putting a CPU on one chip.

People

  • Alan Turing developed the theory of computation and helped break the Enigma code.
  • Grace Hopper developed early compilers, which helped lead to COBOL.
  • Steve Wozniak designed most of the Apple I, released in 1976.
  • Linus Torvalds released the first Linux kernel in 1991.
  • Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web around 1989 to 1991.

Networks and personal computers

ARPANET (1969) demonstrated packet switching and is a direct ancestor of the internet. The IBM PC arrived in 1981, and the first iPhone was released in 2007.

Moore's Law

Gordon Moore observed that the number of transistors on chips roughly doubled about every two years.
